anchor_text: sun with purple-colour'd face
summary: 'Purple' in Elizabethan English meant a deep, blood-red crimson — the color of the sky at dusk or dawn — not the modern violet-blue shade. The sun is personified as a red-faced figure leaving the weeping (dewy) morning behind.
detail: The OED records 'purple' in this period as covering a range from deep red to violet, with the reddish-crimson sense dominant in poetic descriptions of the sky and face. 'Weeping morn' (TLN 2) personifies the dew of dawn as tears, part of the poem's extended pathetic fallacy. The opening stanza sets the pastoral twilight scene before Venus arrives 'amain' (at full speed) in TLN 5.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1
OED s.v. 'purple' adj. does record a reddish-crimson sense dominant in 16th-century poetic descriptions of the sky; the claim accurately reflects the OED entry.

The gloss that 'purple' in Elizabethan usage spans deep red to crimson for the sky/face is sound and well-attested; the personification of 'weeping morn' as dewy dawn is a standard Ovidian pathetic-fallacy reading fully supported by the text.

anchor_text: Sick-thoughted Venus makes amain unto him
summary: 'Sick-thoughted' means consumed, or made sick, by her own thoughts of desire. 'Amain' means at full speed, with all one's force. Venus is not hesitant: she charges directly at Adonis like a soldier at a target.
detail: 'Amain' (OED: 'with full force, at full speed') belongs to the vocabulary of military or nautical urgency — a ship running 'amain' before the wind. Shakespeare uses it here and in the stage plays (e.g. Henry VI) for headlong motion. The stanza's comic shock is the reversal of the usual courtship roles: the goddess pursues the mortal boy like a 'bold-fac'd suitor' (TLN 6), the brazen male wooer of classical comedy turned female.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 5
OED s.v. 'amain' adv. sense 1 and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'amain' are both real, standard references that support the definitions given.

'Sick-thoughted' as love-sick and 'amain' as at full speed are both defensible Elizabethan usages; the comic role-reversal (goddess pursuing mortal) is the poem's explicit conceit, confirmed by 'bold-fac'd suitor' in TLN 6.

anchor_text: Thrice fairer than myself
summary: Venus opens her first speech with a blazon — a formal catalogue of the beloved's beauties. She praises Adonis as fairer than herself (the goddess of beauty), chief flower of the field, a shame ('stain') to all lesser nymphs, whiter and redder than doves or roses. This over-the-top inventory is the classical love-poem's standard opening move.
detail: A 'blazon' (from heraldry: a formal description of a coat of arms) was applied to love-poetry's catalogue of a beloved's charms, listing beauty feature by feature from head to foot. By making Venus, not a male poet, deliver the blazon to a male subject, Shakespeare reverses the Petrarchan convention. 'Stain' here means 'to put in the shade, to outshine' — not to dirty: the beloved's beauty makes lesser beauties look pale. 'More white and red than doves or roses' answers the stock Petrarchan coloring (the lady's white skin, red lips) but applies it to a boy. 'Nature that made thee... at strife with herself' is a stock hyperbole meaning nature could not surpass this masterpiece without destroying it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blazon' n. sense 3: 'A verbal description of a person's qualities, especially as a form of praise'; OED s.v. 'stain' v. sense 4: 'To put to shame by surpassing in excellence.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 7
OED does carry 'blazon' n. in a sense covering verbal description of qualities as praise, and 'stain' v. in a sense of outshining or putting to shame; both senses support the annotation's claims.

Identifying this as a blazon and noting the Petrarchan gender-reversal (Venus cataloguing a male beloved) is mainstream scholarly reading; 'stain' as 'to outshine' is accurately glossed and the hyperbole of Nature at strife is straightforward.

anchor_text: Vouchsafe, thou wonder, to alight thy steed
summary: 'Vouchsafe' means 'condescend to grant' or simply 'be so good as to.' 'Meed' (TLN 15) means reward. Venus is asking Adonis to dismount — and promising that if he does, she will give him a 'meed' of 'honey secrets,' meaning sweet, hidden pleasures.
detail: Both words are common in Elizabethan formal and elevated diction but had already begun to sound archaic by 1593. 'Vouchsafe' retains a feudal-courtly flavor (a superior condescending to a lesser), which is ironic here since Venus is the superior addressing the mortal boy. 'Meed' (OED: 'reward, recompense, bribe') is from Old English; Shakespeare uses it throughout the plays as a dignified word for payment in kind.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 13
OED s.v. 'vouchsafe' v. sense 1 and 'meed' n. sense 1 are standard, well-attested entries that accurately support the definitions given.

'Vouchsafe' as condescend to grant and 'meed' as reward are accurate Elizabethan definitions; the irony of a superior addressing an inferior with courtly deferential language is a defensible interpretive observation.

anchor_text: not cloy thy lips with loath'd satiety
summary: Venus promises Adonis that kissing her will never become boring. 'Cloy' means to disgust by excess — as too much sweet food makes you sick. She promises the opposite: that amid 'plenty' he will still feel 'famished' (craving more), and that she will vary her kisses so constantly that boredom is impossible.
detail: The stanza turns on the paradox of erotic plenty that produces renewed hunger. 'Satiety' (from Latin satietas, fullness to excess) was a medical-erotic commonplace: physicians warned that too much sex exhausted the body, and moralists that erotic satiety led to disgust. Venus's counter-argument — that her love is infinitely various — echoes the 'infinite variety' that Enobarbus later attributes to Cleopatra (Antony and Cleopatra 2.2). The rhetorical figure is antithesis: 'cloy / famish,' 'red and pale,' 'one / twenty,' 'short / long.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 19

The basic gloss of 'cloy' and 'satiety' is sound, but the forward reference to Cleopatra's 'infinite variety' is a speculative cross-play parallel not warranted by this note's scope; the medical-erotic commonplace claim is plausible but asserted without citation, so the detail slightly overreaches.

anchor_text: precedent of pith and livelihood
summary: Venus seizes Adonis's sweating palm and calls it a 'precedent of pith and livelihood' — a proof, or evidence, of vigor and vitality. 'Pith' means core strength or marrow; 'livelihood' here means 'liveliness, vital energy' (not occupation). She treats his palm like an oracle of his virility.
detail: 'Precedent' in this usage means a token or proof (OED sense 1a: 'that which has gone before as an example'). 'Pith' (from the soft marrow of plants and bones) was an Elizabethan metonym for core strength or substance — hence 'pithy' meaning forceful and to the point. 'Livelihood' in the sense of 'liveliness' or 'vital energy' (OED s.v. 'livelihood' sense 2, now obsolete) was already fading by 1593; the modern sense of 'means of living' was the emerging dominant. The whole stanza (TLN 25-30) is comic: desire lends Venus literal physical force to pluck Adonis from his horse.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 26

'Pith' as core strength and 'livelihood' as liveliness/vital energy are both accurate obsolete senses; 'precedent' as token or proof is defensible, and the reading that Venus treats the palm as an omen of virility fits the comic register of the stanza.

anchor_text: leaden appetite, unapt to toy
summary: 'To toy' means to dally or flirt amorously. 'Unapt' means unfit or unwilling. Adonis has a 'leaden appetite' for love — heavy, dull, unresponsive — while Venus burns hot as coals. The contrast between leaden cold and fiery heat is sustained across the next two lines: she is hot with desire, he is red only with shame.
detail: The lead/fire contrast links back to Ovid's Cupid, who struck some with gold arrows (kindling love) and others with lead arrows (quenching it); Adonis reads as a figure struck with lead, Venus with gold. 'Toy' as erotic dalliance is common in Shakespeare (Onions cites multiple uses); 'leaden' carries the weight of the Ovidian arrow motif as well as a general meaning of slow, dull, inert.

'To toy' as amorous dalliance and 'leaden' as dull/inert are uncontroversial; the link to the Ovidian gold/lead arrow dichotomy (Metamorphoses 1.468-474) is a mainstream scholarly reading directly relevant to the poem's Ovidian source.

anchor_text: Backward she push'd him, as she would be thrust
summary: 'Thrust' carries a sexual double meaning throughout Renaissance English. The line says that Venus pushed Adonis backward in the way she herself wished to be physically entered — acting out the desired act in reverse. The wordplay is deliberate: the poem consistently frames Venus's aggression as a displaced enactment of consummation she cannot achieve.
detail: OED records 'thrust' as a standard bawdy term for penetration in the 16th century. The reversal (she pushes; she wishes to be pushed) is the poem's central comic-erotic paradox: the goddess of love, who normally receives, is forced by Adonis's passivity into the male role, yet the phrasing encodes what she actually wants. The next line — 'govern'd him in strength, though not in lust' — separates physical dominance from erotic consent, reinforcing the point that Adonis's body is present but his desire is absent.

anchor_text: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast
summary: This six-line simile compares Venus's kissing to a starving eagle tearing apart its prey. 'Sharp by fast' means made keen by hunger (fasting sharpens the appetite). 'Tires' (TLN 56) is a falconry term meaning 'tears flesh with the beak.' The simile turns her kisses into a predatory feeding rather than a gentle exchange.
detail: 'To tire' (from Old French tirer) was standard falconry vocabulary for a hawk tearing meat (OED s.v. 'tire' v.2: 'to pull, tear, or feed ravenously, as a hawk at its quarry'). Shakespeare uses falconry diction throughout the poem and the plays to characterize Venus. The eagle simile does two things: it makes Venus's affection physically violent and consuming, and it frames Adonis as prey rather than partner. 'Till either gorge be stuff'd or prey be gone' sets the terms of the whole encounter: Venus will not stop until satisfied or until he escapes.

'Tire' as a falconry term for tearing flesh and 'sharp by fast' as keen with hunger are both accurately glossed; the reading of the simile as framing Venus's kisses as predatory consumption rather than tender exchange is fully supported by 'gorge be stuff'd or prey be gone.'

anchor_text: Like a dive-dapper peering through a wave
summary: A 'dive-dapper' (or dabchick) is a small freshwater diving bird that bobs its head up, glances around, and then ducks back under the surface. The simile captures Adonis's tentative movement: he raises his chin as if about to offer the kiss Venus wants, then pulls back just before their lips meet. Comic deflation at its sharpest.
detail: The dive-dapper (little grebe or dabchick, Tachybaptus ruficollis) was a familiar English water-bird known for rapid, nervous submersions. The simile is deliberately bathetic — a goddess is reduced to pursuing someone who behaves like a startled pond-bird. It is one of the poem's recurring comic strategies: high mythological stakes (the goddess of love; a beautiful mortal's fate) are measured against domestic, naturalistic detail (an eagle, a snail, a dive-dapper, a trampling horse). The six-line stanza continues the deflation: when Venus's lips are ready for 'his pay,' Adonis 'winks, and turns his lips another way' (TLN 90) — winks here meaning 'closes his eyes' or 'turns away.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 86

The OED does record 'dive-dapper' n. as a small diving bird (dabchick/little grebe) and cites Venus and Adonis as an early instance; the claim of 'earliest recorded use' is consistent with how the OED entry is commonly reported.

Identifying the dive-dapper as a dabchick/little grebe is correct, the bathos of the simile is clearly operative in context, and the note that 'winks' means closes his eyes rather than winks in the modern sense is an accurate archaic gloss.

anchor_text: I have been woo'd, as I entreat thee now, Even by the stern and direful god of war
summary: Venus boasts that Mars, the god of war — who has never bowed his neck in battle and conquers every fight — was her captive and begged for what Adonis refuses to give freely. She uses Mars's surrender as an argument: if the most violent, unconquerable god yielded to her, how can a boy resist?
detail: The love affair between Venus (Aphrodite) and Mars (Ares) was one of the most famous scandals of classical mythology. Homer's Odyssey (8.266-366) tells how Hephaestus (Vulcan) caught the lovers in a net and exposed them to the laughing gods; Ovid alludes to the liaison throughout. The image of a war-god hanging his lance and shield over the altar of love ('Over my altars hath he hung his lance, / His batter'd shield, his uncontrolled crest,' TLN 103-104) is a standard emblem of arms laid down for love — a real Roman votive tradition (dedicating weapons at a temple). 'Uncontrolled crest' means a helmet-plume never forced to bow. The stanza (TLN 103-108) turns Mars into a domestic figure: he learns 'to sport and dance,' scorns his own 'churlish drum,' and makes Venus's arms ('embrace') his military field and her bed his campaign tent.

sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.171-189 (Golding 1567): the sun-god reveals the Venus-Mars adultery; Hephaestus traps the lovers.

sources.name: Homer, Odyssey

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 97

The Venus-Mars affair is directly invoked in the text and the sources cited (Odyssey 8 and Metamorphoses 4) are the standard classical loci; the votive-dedication reading of arms hung over an altar is a plausible Roman parallel and the domestication of Mars in TLN 105-108 is accurately described.

anchor_text: Love keeps his revels where there are but twain
summary: Venus argues that private, secret lovemaking — 'revels' for only two ('twain') — is not a public transgression. 'Revels' are festive celebrations; Love's celebration requires privacy, not an audience. The blue-veined violets they are lying on cannot betray them.
detail: The stanza (TLN 123-126) offers an argument from nature and secrecy that was a standard move in classical and Renaissance love-rhetoric: the locus amoenus (pleasant place of grass, flowers, and shade) is private and complicit. Venus's claim that 'our sport is not in sight' invokes the pastoral convention that the natural world shelters lovers from society's gaze. 'Twain' is archaic for 'two' (OED s.v. 'twain' adj.: the older form of 'two,' common in verse through the 17th century). 'Blue-vein'd violets' are a precise botanical observation; violets (traditionally associated with love and faithfulness) here serve as the lovers' bower-floor.

The gloss on 'twain' as archaic for two and 'revels' as festive celebration is accurate; reading the stanza as invoking the pastoral locus amoenus convention of nature sheltering lovers is standard and the text clearly supports it ('our sport is not in sight,' 'violets...never can blab').

anchor_text: Love is a spirit all compact of fire
summary: 'Compact of' means 'composed entirely of' or 'made up of.' Renaissance natural philosophy arranged the world into four elements: earth (heavy), water, air, and fire (light). Love, Venus argues, is pure fire — light enough to rise ('aspire'), not heavy ('gross') enough to sink. It is therefore suited to Adonis, not a burden.
detail: The four-element theory (earth, water, air, fire) descended from Aristotle and was foundational to Elizabethan understanding of the natural world, medicine, and psychology. Each element had qualities: fire was hot, dry, and light; earth was cold, dry, and heavy; the 'gross' elements (earth and water) sank, the lighter (air and fire) rose. Venus uses the science to rebut Adonis's implied objection that love is too heavy: love, she says, does not sink but 'aspires' (rises). The word 'gross' means heavy, coarse, or solid (OED s.v. 'gross' adj. sense 6: 'not refined; dense, solid, heavy'). The argument reinforces her offer to float or dance weightlessly (TLN 146-148).

'Compact of' as composed of is accurately glossed, the four-element theory is correctly described, and the reading that Venus uses elemental science to rebut an implied objection that love is too heavy is directly grounded in TLN 149-150 and the surrounding stanzas.

anchor_text: Narcissus so himself himself forsook, And died to kiss his shadow in the brook
summary: Narcissus was a beautiful youth in Ovid's Metamorphoses who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away unable to possess it, finally dying and turning into a flower. Venus uses the myth to warn Adonis: loving only his own beauty, like Narcissus, leads to self-destruction rather than fulfillment.
detail: Ovid tells the story in Metamorphoses 3.339-510; Arthur Golding's English translation (1567) was Shakespeare's working text. Narcissus had rejected every lover, including the nymph Echo, and was cursed to desire only what he could never have — his own image. 'Himself himself forsook' catches the paradox of Narcissus: in pursuing only himself he destroyed himself. The doubled pronoun ('himself himself') is a characteristic Shakespearean compression of the self-defeating logic. Venus deploys the myth as a cautionary exemplum: self-absorbed refusal of love is not chastity but a kind of death. The same myth appears in the Sonnets to admonish the self-absorbed Fair Youth (Sonnet 1).

sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-510 (Golding 1567): Narcissus falls in love with his reflection and pines away; the flower named for him springs from the spot where he died.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 161
Ovid Metamorphoses 3.339-510 (Golding 1567) is the confirmed correct location for the Echo and Narcissus episode; the line range is verified by multiple academic sources.

The Narcissus myth from Ovid Metamorphoses 3 is the direct source; 'himself himself forsook' as expressing the paradox of self-defeating self-pursuit is sound and the application as a cautionary exemplum against self-absorbed refusal of love is exactly what Venus's rhetoric at this point requires.

anchor_text: Seeds spring from seeds, and beauty breedeth beauty; Thou wast begot; to get it is thy duty
summary: Venus closes her first major speech with the procreation argument: since Adonis himself was begotten (conceived), he has a duty to beget — to reproduce — in turn. Beauty, like seed, must be planted in another to survive. Refusing sex is not just personal but a failure of natural obligation.
detail: This is the exact argument Shakespeare will later develop across Sonnets 1-17 ('From fairest creatures we desire increase' — Sonnet 1). The logic is biological and moral at once: beauty is a form of natural wealth held in trust; to let it die childless is to waste it. 'To get' means 'to beget, to father or conceive a child' (OED s.v. 'get' v. sense 9: 'to beget'). The final line of the scene has the compressed authority of a proverb: cause and duty in two clauses. 'Things growing to themselves are growth's abuse' (TLN 166) extends the argument into natural philosophy: individual creatures that grow only for themselves (no offspring, no community, no use) corrupt the purpose of growth itself.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 167

'To get' as to beget is a standard archaic usage, the procreation argument is the explicit rhetorical content of the stanza, and the parallel with Sonnets 1-17 is legitimate since Venus and Adonis and the Sonnets are widely held to be roughly contemporaneous works deploying the same procreation topos.

anchor_text: law of nature thou art bound to breed
summary: Venus delivers the procreation argument: nature's law obliges every living creature to reproduce so that it survives in its offspring after death. The same logic drives Shakespeare's first seventeen sonnets, urging the Fair Youth to marry and have children.
detail: The opening stanza of this scene completes a Venus speech that began earlier in the poem. 'Increase' means both the earth's crops and the offspring of a creature; the wordplay ties Adonis's body to fertile land. The logic is Epicurean and Stoic commonplace (Cicero, De Finibus 5.9; Erasmus, Epistle in Praise of Marriage), but also Ovidian: Ovid's Venus in Metamorphoses 10 argues from pleasure not nature. Shakespeare reverses this, making his Venus a moralist-in-despite-of-herself, whose cleverest arguments are also the most absurd given her purely erotic purpose.

anchor_text: Titan, tired in the mid-day heat
summary: Titan is a poetic name for the sun-god (Helios or Phoebus Apollo). Here the narrator imagines the sun growing weary and jealous, wishing he could swap places with Adonis to lie beside Venus.
detail: In Hesiod's Theogony the Titans are the older generation of gods; Helios the Sun is their descendant. By Shakespeare's day 'Titan' was used interchangeably for the sun itself in poetry (cf. Golding's Ovid passim). The conceit — that the sun himself envies Adonis — escalates the poem's theme of universal desire directed at the youth: even a god cannot resist him. Golding uses 'Titan' for the sun throughout his 1567 translation, making it a standard poetic label known to any reader of Ovid.

'Titan' as a poetic synonym for the sun, transmitted through Golding's Ovid, is well-attested; the conceit of the sun envying Adonis is clearly what lines 177-180 say.

summary: 'Spright' is an Elizabethan spelling of 'spirit,' here meaning Adonis's mood or disposition — his listless, unwilling state of mind. The narrator piles up words for his sulky reluctance: lazy, heavy, dark, disliking.

For a reader who knows Ovid's story, the line is deeply ironic: Adonis's preference for hunting a boar over pursuing love is exactly the choice that kills him. He will chase a wild boar, it will gore him to death, and his blood will become a flower — the Ovidian ending this poem is moving toward.
detail: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.708-739 (Golding 1567), Venus warns Adonis to hunt only safe prey and spare the boar, but he ignores her and is killed. Shakespeare shifts the irony earlier: Adonis's casual dismissal ('unless it be a boar, and then I chase it') is also an unwitting prophecy. The boar is a standard emblem of violence and dangerous masculinity in classical and Renaissance hunting literature; Adonis's equation of hunting-excitement with the only 'love' he values makes him choose his own death.

anchor_text: Remove your siege from my unyielding heart: To love's alarms it will not ope the gate
summary: Adonis uses a sustained military metaphor: his heart is a fortified town under siege, Venus is the besieging army, her vows and tears are weapons ('alarms' = calls to attack), and he tells her to give up the assault because no 'battery' (cannon fire) will breach his walls. The extended metaphor frames his refusal as military honour rather than mere coldness.
detail: In Elizabethan military terminology: 'siege' = the surrounding of a fortified place; 'alarms' = calls to arms or charges; 'battery' = the battering of walls with artillery. All three terms were active in late-16th-century siege warfare (e.g. the sieges of the Low Countries wars). The metaphor is ironic in context: love-poetry routinely cast courtship as siege warfare (compare Sidney, Astrophil and Stella), so Adonis is appropriating a convention usually used by the lover against the beloved and turning it against Venus herself.

anchor_text: Thy mermaid's voice hath done me double wrong; I had my load before, now press'd with bearing
summary: Venus calls Adonis's voice a 'mermaid's voice' — the deadly sweet singing of the Sirens, who in classical myth lured sailors to their deaths with irresistible song. She means the paradox that his speaking is a second wound: before he spoke she was already in pain from his cold looks; his beautiful voice has now made it worse. 'Mermaid' in Elizabethan English was used interchangeably with 'siren.'
detail: In Homer's Odyssey (12.39-54, 165-200) the Sirens lure sailors with song that promises perfect knowledge; Odysseus is tied to the mast to hear and survive. In Renaissance usage 'mermaid' often replaced 'siren,' the two figures blending into a single image of fatal feminine beauty and voice. Venus deploys the allusion with characteristic self-awareness: she is the goddess who ought to lure others, yet here she is the one ensnared by a mortal boy's voice.

anchor_text: For from the stillitory of thy face excelling Comes breath perfum'd that breedeth love by smelling
summary: A 'stillitory' (also spelled 'stillatorie') is a distillery — an apparatus used in alchemy and medicine to extract essences and perfumes from flowers or herbs by distillation. Venus says Adonis's face is like a distillery from which his very breath emerges as a concentrated perfume, and that this perfumed breath is enough to breed love through the sense of smell alone. The image belongs to the poem's argument that all five senses lead to love.

Distillation was a common household and apothecary practice in the late 16th century, used to make rosewater, herbal medicines, and perfumes; Shakespeare uses the same distillation metaphor for beauty in Sonnet 5 ('beauty's legacy... beauty's effect with beauty were bereft, / Nor it nor no remembrance what it was'). Venus is working through all five senses (sight, touch, hearing, smell, taste) across stanzas 433-450, and this stanza belongs to 'smell.'

anchor_text: Once more the ruby-colour'd portal open'd, Which to his speech did honey passage yield, Like a red morn, that ever yet betoken'd Wrack to the seaman

But the narrator immediately undercuts the beauty: the red mouth is like a red morning sky, which sailors read as a warning of storm ('Wrack' = shipwreck or destruction). The simile converts a conventional blazon of physical beauty into a bad omen, foreshadowing that what Adonis is about to say will cause Venus harm.

'Wrack' = wreck (of ships); 'flaws' = gusts or squalls.

anchor_text: Do I delight to die, or life desire? But now I liv'd, and life was death's annoy; But now I died, and death was lively joy
summary: Venus uses tight antithesis — opposites placed side by side — to describe her swoon and revival: being alive was painful ('death's annoy'), and fainting (a little death) was joyful. 'Annoy' means injury or torment, not mere irritation. The paradox also plays on the Petrarchan convention of the 'little death' (Italian: la petite morte) — the idea that intense passion, including the faint, temporarily suspends the self.
detail: The passage is an example of the rhetorical figure chiasmus: 'I lived... death's annoy / I died... lively joy' — the terms cross (life/death, death/life) as in an X shape. The antithetical stanza structure, with 'But now... But now' as the pivot, was a favourite of the Petrarchan erotic tradition descending through the Italian sonnet and Sidney's Astrophil and Stella. 'Annoy' in Elizabethan English was stronger than in modern usage: it could mean injury, trouble, or serious torment (OED s.v. 'annoy' n. 2).

anchor_text: sweet seals in my soft lips imprinted
summary: Venus sustains an extended commercial metaphor over six lines: lips are wax seals that stamp agreements, kisses are 'bargains,' and Adonis's touching her again is 'sealing' the deal. A 'seal-manual' (TLN 516) was a personal seal made by pressing the hand or a signet ring into hot wax to authenticate a legal document. Venus frames seduction as a binding contract.

Venus exploits each term: 'bargains,' 'sell,' 'buy and pay,' 'good dealing,' 'purchase,' 'slips' (counterfeit coins), and 'seal-manual' all belong to the language of trade and legal obligation. The conceit turns an erotic advance into what looks like a fair transaction, neutralising Adonis's moral resistance. 'Wax-red lips' (TLN 516) simultaneously names the wax for sealing and Venus's flushed mouth. The six-line stanza locks this device to the stanza form of the whole poem.

anchor_text: Measure my strangeness with my unripe years
summary: Adonis asks Venus to judge his reluctance ('strangeness') by his youth ('unripe years') — he is too young to understand love, let alone himself ('Before I know myself, seek not to know me'). He backs the argument with two nature comparisons: a fisherman lets small fry ('ungrown fry') go free, and a green plum clings to the branch and tastes sour if picked early. 'Strangeness' here means coldness or aloofness toward a wooer, not unfamiliarity.
detail: The pairing of 'ungrown fry' (immature fish, too small to keep) and the unripe plum is a rhetorical device called similitudo — two parallel illustrations making the same point. Both images insist that premature harvest defeats itself: the fry is discarded because it has not grown; the plum is sour because it has not ripened. Adonis applies the same logic to his own emotional and sexual unreadiness. The poem overall reverses Ovid's version, in which Adonis is a willing partner; Shakespeare's Adonis is genuinely, not coyly, reluctant.

anchor_text: blindfold fury she begins to forage
summary: The narrator shifts from Venus as military victor to Venus as an animal foraging blindly for food. Her face 'reeks and smokes' (steams with heat — 'reek' is not yet a term for foul smell here), her blood boils, and 'careless lust' — desire that ignores consequences — pushes out reason ('beating reason back') and shame. The rapid catalogue of body, blood, and mind becoming disordered shows lust as a force that overrides every faculty.
detail: In Elizabethan physiology, passion was understood to heat the blood, which then overwhelmed the rational soul. 'Reek and smoke' describes the steaming of overheated flesh (compare the face of a horse after a race). 'Blindfold fury' adapts the standard iconography of Cupid blindfolded (see cupid-arrows), but here the blindness is Venus's own: her desire makes her heedless ('careless') of outcome. 'Forgetting shame's pure blush and honour's wrack' identifies the two things lust destroys: the modest shame that regulates behaviour, and the care for reputation ('honour').

anchor_text: birds, deceiv'd with painted grapes
summary: The simile refers to the ancient story of the painter Zeuxis, who supposedly painted grapes so realistically that birds flew down to peck at them. Shakespeare turns it into a figure for thwarted appetite: the eye sends a message of plenty that the body cannot fulfil, exactly Venus's situation. 'Pine the maw' = cause the stomach to waste away.

anchor_text: On his bow-back he hath a battle set
summary: Venus delivers a set-piece portrait of the boar as a military force: its arched back ('bow-back') is like a battlefield ('battle') of bristling spears ('bristly pikes'), its eyes glow like worms when it is angry, its snout digs graves wherever it goes, and it attacks anything in its path. The boar was a conventional emblem of savage, undeflectable force in classical and Renaissance poetry. Ovid's description of the Calydonian boar in Metamorphoses 8 is the immediate model.
detail: Ovid describes the Calydonian boar's bristles like iron spears, eyes glowing like fire, and destructive charge at Metamorphoses 8.284-290 (Golding 1567). The boar's geological destructiveness ('snout digs sepulchres') anticipates how it will actually kill Adonis — by goring — and makes its whole body a weapon. anchor_text: purblind hare
summary: 'Purblind' means nearly blind or dim-sighted; hares were proverbially short-sighted. anchor_text: misery is trodden on by many, And being low never reliev'd by any
summary: These two lines step out of the narrative to deliver a senten tia — a self-contained moral maxim, one of classical rhetoric's most valued ornaments. The maxim pities the wretch so far below that no one bends to help: misfortune is kicked by those who pass over it, and those who are already low get no relief. The couplet briefly opens the hare-chase into a general truth about suffering and indifference.

Classical and Renaissance rhetorical training (after Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 8.5) taught schoolboys to recognise and produce them; they often appear at the end of an argument in rhymed pairs (here an ababcc stanza closes with a gnomic cc couplet). Shakespeare is here doing exactly what his grammar-school rhetoric master taught: ending a descriptive passage with a pithy universal. The conceit also foreshadows Venus's own helplessness later in the scene, when Adonis walks away and she can do nothing to hold him.

anchor_text: hath she brib'd the Destinies

The argument these stanzas make — that beauty is mortal and vulnerable to disease, age, and mishap, and therefore must reproduce itself before being destroyed — closely parallels the argument of Shakespeare's Sonnets 1-17 (the 'procreation sonnets'), in which the young man's beauty is warned to breed before it fades.

anchor_text: she beats her heart, whereat it groans

anchor_text: Hard-favour'd tyrant, ugly, meagre, lean, Hateful divorce of love
summary: This is an apostrophe — a rhetorical figure in which a speaker addresses an absent or abstract entity as if it were present. anchor_text: The Destinies will curse thee for this stroke

anchor_text: beauty dead, black chaos comes again

anchor_text: Who, like a king perplexed in his throne, By their suggestion gives a deadly groan, Whereat each tributary subject quakes

anchor_text: Bonnet nor veil henceforth no creature wear
summary: Venus bans bonnets and veils because they were worn partly to protect the complexion from the sun and wind — the very elements that 'lurk'd like two thieves' to steal Adonis's beauty. Now that the most beautiful face is gone, there is nothing left worth protecting; the sun will scorn other faces rather than covet them.
detail: The extended conceit (TLN 1081-1092) works on a quasi-mythological premise: when Adonis was alive, the sun and wind were like jealous admirers who would peep under his hat-brim to glimpse his face and then quarrel to dry his tears. The 'bonnet' is a broad-brimmed hat, worn both by men and (in different styles) by women in Elizabethan England, primarily against weather. The passage is one of the poem's most playful extravagances: nature personified as star-struck voyeurs, and death as the event that strips the world of beauty so completely that even vanity becomes pointless.

anchor_text: When he beheld his shadow in the brook, The fishes spread on it their golden gills
summary: When Adonis looked at his own reflection in the brook, the fish came and spread their bright fins over the image, as if adoring it. The moment echoes the myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool — but here nature adores Adonis, not Adonis himself.
detail: In Ovid's Metamorphoses 3.339-510, Narcissus pines and dies over his own image in the water. Venus earlier accused Adonis of a Narcissus-like refusal to love (lines 161-162: 'Narcissus so himself himself forsook, / And died to kiss his shadow in the brook'). Now the same brook-image returns, but inverted: at TLN 1099-1100 the fish adore the reflection that Adonis himself ignores, externalising the desire his modesty suppresses. This is one of many moments where the poem's earlier arguments re-echo in the lament.

anchor_text: this foul, grim, and urchin-spouted boar, Whose downward eye still looketh for a grave
summary: 'Urchin-spouted' means having a snout like a hedgehog's — 'urchin' was the Elizabethan word for a hedgehog. The boar's 'downward eye' (TLN 1106) means its gaze is directed to the ground, as rooting animals look down. Venus is building a picture of the boar as ugly, earth-bound, and death-seeking — the antithesis of sky-gazing, beauty-loving Adonis.

The line makes the boar's very anatomy an emblem of death: downward-looking animals in bestiaries and emblem books were types of the earthbound and the mortal.

anchor_text: He thought to kiss him, and hath killed him so
summary: Venus reinterprets the boar's killing as a misdirected lover's kiss: the animal pressed its face into Adonis's flank meaning to kiss him, but its tusks went in 'unaware.' The reinterpretation is Venus's desperate defence of Adonis from the charge of having been killed — and a self-accusatory aside ('Had I been tooth'd like him, I must confess, / With kissing him I should have kill'd him first').
detail: The passage (TLN 1111-1120) is the poem's most sustained exercise in erotic mortification: Venus projects her own uncontrolled desire onto the boar, whose 'nuzzling in his flank' and 'sheath'd unaware the tusk in his soft groin' conflate the act of killing with the act of sexual penetration. 'Groin' (TLN 1116) is anatomically exact and loaded. The boar becomes Venus's surrogate — it succeeded in the penetrating intimacy she was denied. The self-accusation that follows ('Had I been tooth'd like him... With kissing him I should have killed him first') implicates Venus in the death through the very excess of her desire. Editors including Katherine Duncan-Jones and Henry Woudhuysen, eds., Shakespeare's Poems (Arden 3rd series, 2007), note the deliberate conflation of desire and destruction throughout this episode.

anchor_text: She lifts the coffer-lids that close his eyes, Where, lo! two lamps, burnt out, in darkness lies
summary: Venus lifts Adonis's eyelids as if opening the lids of a treasure chest ('coffer-lids'), only to find not jewels but 'two lamps, burnt out, in darkness.' The image shifts from a casket of riches (suggesting the priceless worth of his eyes) to extinguished lights, in three words making the transition from hope to desolation.
detail: A 'coffer' was a locked chest for valuables; 'coffer-lids' for eyelids is a sustained metaphor that treats the eyes as the greatest treasure the body contains. In the previous stanza (TLN 1129-1130) the eyes become 'two glasses' (mirrors) in which Venus beheld herself 'a thousand times, and now no more reflect.' Shakespeare accumulates three distinct metaphors for the dead eyes in two stanzas: jewel-box, lamps, and mirrors. Each measures a different kind of loss — beauty, illumination, self-reflection — and together they constitute a blazon of grief inverting the conventional love-poet's blazon of beauty.

anchor_text: Since thou art dead, lo! here I prophesy, Sorrow on love hereafter shall attend
summary: Venus delivers a formal curse on love itself — a prophecy that from this moment on, love will be inseparable from jealousy, sorrow, fraud, and disappointment. This seven-stanza speech (TLN 1135-1164) is a 'complaint' speech, a set rhetorical genre in which a grieving figure curses the condition that destroyed her. It also functions as an etiology — an explanation of why love is painful.
detail: An etiology (or aetiological myth) explains how a present condition came to be. Ovid's Metamorphoses is full of them: Narcissus becomes the flower; Philomela becomes the nightingale. Here Venus's curse explains why love is the paradoxical, self-tormenting thing that sonnets and love-complaints describe. The speech covers almost every contradiction of Petrarchan love-poetry: hot/cold, high/low, fickle/constant, fierce/mild, war-making/peace-making. As a formal oration it mirrors Venus's earlier wooing speeches in length and structure — but where those were attempts to win Adonis, this one is a pronouncement of permanent cosmic damage. The speech ends the poem's movement; what follows is only the metamorphosis and the closing frame.

anchor_text: Was melted like a vapour from her sight, And in his blood that on the ground lay spill'd, A purple flower sprung up, chequer'd with white
summary: Adonis's body vanishes like mist and a flower — purple with white markings, its colours matching his pale cheeks and the dark blood — springs from the spilled blood. This is the poem's central metamorphosis, taken from Ovid: the anemone that grows from Adonis's blood.
detail: Ovid tells in Metamorphoses 10.735-739 (Golding 1567) that Venus sprinkles Adonis's blood with nectar and within an hour a flower springs up — the short-lived anemone, whose name (from Greek anemos, wind) signals that it blooms and falls with the wind. Shakespeare changes the flower from the anemone to something 'chequer'd with white' on purple, generally taken to be the anemone coronaria, whose dark petals are often marked with a paler centre, though some editors also suggest a windflower. The motif of a body dissolving 'like a vapour' belongs to the same Ovidian world of transformation: matter does not die but changes shape. The poem's final two stanzas enact the metamorphosis as a culminating act of Ovidian craft, the poem completing the myth it began with.

anchor_text: this was thy father's guise, Sweet issue
summary: 'Guise' means custom or habitual manner (OED s.v. 'guise', n., sense 2a). 'Issue' means offspring or child. Venus addresses the anemone flower as though it were Adonis's own child, saying weeping at every small grief was its father's way, and so the flower has inherited it.
detail: The paradox Venus constructs here is that Adonis is simultaneously the flower's father (his blood generated it) and himself transformed into it. By calling it his 'issue,' she folds the Ovidian metamorphosis into the language of inheritance: the flower does not merely spring from Adonis's body but continues his lineage. 'Sweet-smelling sire' plays on the flower's scent as a literal trait the child has received. The grief-and-weeping motif — 'for every little grief to wet his eyes' — retrospectively explains why Adonis wept at Venus's rhetoric earlier in the poem; the line makes his coldness a matter of temperament, not cruelty.

anchor_text: To grow unto himself was his desire
summary: Growing 'unto himself' — turning inward, wanting only oneself — recalls the myth of Narcissus, the youth who fell in love with his own reflection and wasted away. Earlier in the poem (line 161) Venus had warned Adonis directly: 'Narcissus so himself himself forsook, / And died to kiss his shadow in the brook.' The flower's nature mirrors its father's self-enclosure.
detail: Ovid's Narcissus (Metamorphoses 3.339-510; Golding's English translation, 1567) was the standard Tudor emblem of sterile self-regard: the youth who spurned all lovers, fell for his own image, and was eventually changed into the narcissus flower. Shakespeare uses the allusion twice in the poem: as a warning (line 161, Venus argues that refusing love is Narcissus's error) and here, as an epitaph — the anemone flower 'grows unto itself,' completing the Narcissus parallel. The phrase also anticipates the procreation sonnets, where an unnamed self-absorbed young man is told that 'thou contracted to thine own bright eyes / Feed'st thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel' (Sonnet 1), almost the same charge.
